newsitem.title: PERU: Peru readies new proposal as rebels reject asylum.
newsitem.headline: Peru readies new proposal as rebels reject asylum.

text.p: Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori said on Tuesday the government is preparing an "all-inclusive proposal" to Marxist rebels who have rejected government moves to lure them into asylum to end a 77-day-old hostage siege.

Fujimori spoke in the southern city of Arequipa hours after guerrilla leader Nestor Cerpa dashed hopes that he and his 20-odd comrades would accept one-way tickets to Cuba in return for dropping their main demands.

The president said that the government was not giving up either the search for a bloodless end to the siege or its stance against ceding to the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) demands for the release of 400 jailed comrades.

"His (Cerpa's) reactions are known publicly and we are not going to respond to his reactions," Fujimori said. "The government is preparing an all-inclusive proposal as a result of the talks that have been held in seven or eight meetings."

Cerpa said earlier in a walkie-talkie conversation monitored by Reuters that the eight rounds of talks between rebels and government have so far led only to both sides entrenching themselves behind their positions.

Speaking from his stronghold within the captured Japanese ambassador's Lima residence, Cerpa ruled out accepting a possible offer for asylum in the Dominican Republic but refused to comment on Monday's offer of sanctuary by Cuban leader Fidel Castro.

"Our first priority is to stay in our fatherland, which is the path we have chosen to fight at the side of our people," he said, adding "We have no intention of looking for exile or asylum in the Dominican Republic, and even less in any country that oppresses its people."

"With respect to the Cuban government's willingness to take us in, we consider it appropriate not to make a comment right now to avoid our words being distorted. We do this out of respect for the Cuban government, Commander Fidel Castro, his revolution and his people."
Cerpa said that the rebels were sticking to their demand for the release of prisoners to end Latin America's longest-running hostage siege.
"But we believe this (the talks) cannot continue indefinitely in the sense that they can get worn down and lose a certain level of legitimacy," he said.
Cerpa added that the stalemate led him to decide not to attend the eighth round of talks on Monday, sending instead his deputy, Rolly Rojas.
But, on the other side of the bargaining table, Fujimori was equally intransigent.
"There has been no proposal for an amnesty (for rebels) presented to Congress and no proposal for an amnesty for the MRTA prisoners," he said in Arequipa.
Fujimori has hinted at other concessions, possibly including a softening of the harsh conditions for MRTA prisoners and a reform of trial processes.
The ninth round of talks is due to be held on Wednesday.
Castro confirmed he would accept the MRTA fighters out of a "moral duty" and "not a question of convenience." The MRTA draws its inspiration from the 1959 Cuban revolution.

The proposal drew immediate backing from Tokyo, whose cooperation is essential to any solution. Japanese officials said Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto would seek support from the United States, an avowed enemy of Cuba, for the proposal.
The MRTA are holding 72 hostages -- including Fujimori's brother Pedro, two government ministers and the envoys of Japan and Bolivia -- in the luxurious diplomatic mansion.
They seized their captives in a spectacular raid on a cocktail party to celebrate the Japanese Emperor's birthday on Dec. 17.
